chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad, from Muʿallā ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, who said:

I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: How much is taʿzīr? He said: “Less than the hadd.” He said: I said: Less than eighty? He said: “No, rather it is less than forty, for that is the hadd of the slave.” He said: I said: And how much is that? He said: “ʿAlī عليه السلام said: According to the measure that the governor sees of the man’s offense and the strength of his body.”

So the first point in it is that it is not apparent in the outward wording of the report that the hadd of the slave, which is forty, is only in his drinking wine. And when that is not apparent in its wording, it is permissible that this be his hadd in matters other than it. Even if it were explicit that this is his hadd in drinking wine, it would be permissible for us to interpret it as a form of taqiyyah, because that agrees with the doctrine of some of the ʿāmmah.

key_terms.التَّعْزِيرُ: discretionary punishment set below a fixed hadd penalty
key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary conformity in circumstances of risk
key_terms.الْأَرْبَعِينَ: forty lashes, mentioned here as an upper boundary in this discussion
key_terms.الْمَمْلُوكِ: the slave, whose legal hadd is referenced in the report
key_terms.الْوَالِي: the governing authority or ruler who assesses the punishment
key_terms.ذَنْبِ: the offense or sin committed by the person
key_terms.قُوَّةِ بَدَنِهِ: the physical strength of the offender, considered in determining taʿzīr

ai.seo_question: How many lashes may be given in taʿzīr according to Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام?
ai.summary: This report discusses the legal scope of taʿzīr, stating that it must remain below the fixed hadd punishment and specifically below forty lashes. It further attributes to Amīr al-Muʾminīn ʿAlī عليه السلام that the exact amount is left to the judgment of the ruler based on the offense and the offender’s physical capacity. The closing passage explains a juristic reading of the report and notes the possibility of taqiyyah in interpreting the statement about the slave’s hadd.
